# Kawahara capillary–gravity waves {#sec-kawahara}

`apps/kawahara` — the only *dispersive* model in the report: fifth order, and
its linear symbol is purely imaginary.

## Physical setting

Long weakly nonlinear waves on a shallow fluid layer where surface tension and
gravity both matter. Where the Korteweg–de Vries equation keeps only
third-order dispersion, @Kawahara1972 retains the fifth-order term as well.
When the two have opposite signs they compete, and the resulting dispersion
relation is non-monotonic — waves of different length can travel in opposite
directions.

Two physical questions follow, and the application answers them with separate
runs. The first is linear and kinematic: **release a wave packet on such a
layer — at what speed does its envelope travel, and at what speed do the
crests inside it travel?** Below the crossover those two answers have the same
sign and above it they do not. The observables are the **group velocity**,
measured from the drift of the envelope centroid, and the **phase velocity**,
measured from the phase of the carrier's own Fourier coefficient.

The second question is nonlinear: **what does the fifth-order term actually
do?** Switching $\gamma$ off reduces the equation to KdV, which has an exact
solitary wave that propagates forever unchanged. Running the *same* solitary
wave with $\gamma$ restored makes every departure from that behaviour
attributable to $\gamma$ alone. The observables are the **solitary-wave peak
amplitude and propagation speed**, the **RMS amplitude of the trailing
radiation**, and the **dominant wavenumber of that radiation**, which linear
theory predicts from the resonance $c_p(k) = c$.

## Problem setup

Three configurations, and they are not interchangeable. `pulse.json` and the
mode tests are the **verification preset**: arbitrary hand-picked coefficients,
exercised against closed-form phase and amplitude. They are a numerical oracle
and **not a production science case**. Science cases A and B use coefficients
derived from a documented capillary–gravity mapping.

| Item | Verification preset | Science case A (wave packet) | Science case B (solitary wave) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Use case | Exercise $L(k) = -i(\beta k^3 + \gamma k^5)$ against independently derived phase | Capillary–gravity wave-packet dispersion just below the critical Bond number | Loss of KdV integrability to fifth-order dispersion, at the same Bond number |
| Domain | 1-D periodic line, $N_x = 64$–$256$; $L_x = 64\pi$ for `pulse.json` | 1-D periodic line, $N_x = 2560$, $L_x = 800$ | 1-D periodic line, $N_x = 512$, $L_x = 128$ |
| Grid | $\Delta x = \pi/4$ to $\pi/2$; $N_y = N_z = 1$ throughout | $\Delta x = 0.3125$; $t \in [0, 250]$, sampled every 5 | $\Delta x = 0.25$ — 13 points across the solitary wave and 16 across the radiated wavelength; $t \in [0, 100]$ at $\Delta t = 0.005$ |
| Boundary conditions | Periodic; the spectral stack has no other mode | Periodic, but sized so the packet never reaches the boundary, with an `edge_fraction` sentinel checking that every sample | Periodic, and the radiation *does* wrap before $t = 100$ — see below |
| Initial condition | `cosine_mode`, or `gaussian_pulse` ($A = 0.4$, $\sigma = 6$, centred) | `wave_packet`: Gaussian-envelope carrier, $\sigma = 15$, $x_0 = 150$, at $k_0 = 0.6990$ (below crossover) or $k_0 = 2.0028$ (above), each an exact grid mode | `kdv_soliton`: $A\,\mathrm{sech}^2((x-x_0-ct)/W)$ with $A = 0.05$, $x_0 = 32$; $c$ and $W$ are **derived from $\alpha$ and $\beta$**, so an input cannot silently stop being a solution |
| Key physical parameters | $\alpha = 1$, $\beta = 1$, $\gamma = -1$ — nondimensional and hand-picked, with no physical mapping | $h = g = 1$, $\tau = 0.30$ giving $\alpha = 1.5$, $\beta = -1/60$, $\gamma = 1/90$; $\alpha$ is then set to 0 to isolate the linear dispersion | Same mapping, full $\alpha = 1.5$, $\beta = -1/60$; $\gamma = 0$ (control) against $\gamma = 1/90$ |
| Observable | Phase and amplitude against the analytical cosine solution; mean $u$ | Group velocity from envelope centroid drift, phase velocity from the carrier mode, packet width, `edge_fraction` | Peak amplitude, peak position, trailing-radiation RMS, dominant radiation wavenumber, mean $u$ |
| Model maturity | numerical verification: **analytical** · physical completeness: **canonical** — the Kawahara equation exercised as an equation · calibration: **none** | numerical verification: **analytical** for the phase velocity, **regression** for the group velocity · physical completeness: **reduced** — 1-D, weakly nonlinear, long-wave asymptotics · calibration: **representative**, see below | numerical verification: **analytical** — amplitude, width, speed and radiation wavenumber all come from closed forms, not stored values — plus **regression** for the tail RMS · physical completeness: **reduced**, as beside · calibration: **representative** |

Periodicity means a closed ring of fluid rather than an open channel: no
wavemaker, no inflow, no outflow. Because $L(k)$ is purely imaginary the model
has no dissipation at all, so nothing that leaves one end is ever absorbed — it
re-enters at the other. The two science cases handle that differently, and the
difference is worth stating rather than glossing. Case A is sized from the
analytical group velocity so the packet cannot approach the boundary, and the
`edge_fraction` sentinel proves it: the envelope in the outer 5 % of the domain
stays below $10^{-7}$ of the peak at every sample. **Case B makes no such
claim** — its radiation does wrap before $t = 100$. That is harmless for the
observables it uses, because whole-domain tail RMS and its dominant wavenumber
do not care where in the box the radiation sits, but no no-wrap statement can
be made for it. What the idealisation excludes throughout is everything a real
channel has and this model does not: viscous damping, a bottom boundary layer,
sidewalls, and wave breaking.

### Capillary–gravity parameter mapping

Depth $h$, gravity $g$ and Bond number $\tau = T/(\rho g h^2)$ map to the
equation's coefficients, in a frame moving at the linear long-wave speed
$c_0 = \sqrt{gh}$, as

$$
\alpha = \frac{3c_0}{2h}, \qquad
\beta  = \frac{c_0h^2}{6}\,(3\tau - 1), \qquad
\gamma = \frac{c_0h^4}{90}.
$$ {#eq-kw-map}

$\gamma$ is always positive; $\beta$ is negative — competing dispersion, with a
real crossover at $k_c = \sqrt{-\beta/\gamma}$ — below the critical Bond number
$\tau = 1/3$, and positive above it.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Provenance of @eq-kw-map

This mapping was assembled from secondary and tertiary literature summaries,
not from the primary sources, which were not accessible from the machine the
work was done on. The prefactors recur consistently across the independent
secondary sources consulted, but they have not been re-derived from the Euler
water-wave equations or checked against a primary paper here. Treat it as
**representative** of the documented capillary–gravity regime, not as a
quantitative, primary-source-verified calibration.
:::

### Measured: wave-packet dispersion

At $\tau = 0.30$ the crossover sits at $k_c \approx 1.2247$, and the two
carriers straddle it.

| $k_0$ | side | $d\omega/dk$ analytic | $v_g$ measured | $c_p$ analytic | $c_p$ measured | max `edge_fraction` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.6990 | below $k_c$ | $-0.011167$ | $-0.010915$ (2.3 %) | $-0.005491$ | $-0.005491$ ($\sim10^{-14}$) | $9.3\times10^{-9}$ |
| 2.0028 | above $k_c$ | $0.693258$ | $0.696118$ (0.4 %) | $0.111911$ | $0.111911$ ($\sim10^{-14}$) | $1.0\times10^{-8}$ |

The phase velocity agrees to machine precision, as it must: the carrier is an
exact grid mode and the linear ETD step advances it exactly. The group velocity
agrees to a few percent, which is the accuracy of the narrowband envelope
extraction rather than of the solver.

### Measured: a solitary wave forced to radiate

With $\gamma = 0$ the equation is KdV with dispersion coefficient
$\delta = -\beta$, and the `kdv_soliton` initial condition is its exact
travelling solution. That is the control: it should propagate indefinitely
unchanged, so every departure in the $\gamma \ne 0$ run is attributable to
$\gamma$. The solitary wave is resonant with the linear waves whose phase
velocity equals its own, $c_p(k) = \beta k^2 + \gamma k^4 = c$, which for
$\beta < 0 < \gamma$ has exactly one positive root — here
$k_{\mathrm{res}} = 1.5579$. Nothing in the solver is told that number.

| Quantity at $t = 100$ | KdV control ($\gamma = 0$) | Full Kawahara ($\gamma = 1/90$) |
|---|---|---|
| Peak amplitude | 0.050007 (from 0.05) | 0.035986 |
| Distance travelled | 2.50, against $cT = 2.50$ | — |
| Trailing RMS | $4.19\times10^{-5}$ (the $\mathrm{sech}^2$ skirt) | $3.13\times10^{-3}$ (75×) |
| Dominant tail wavenumber | 0.049 — the lowest mode in the box, i.e. no wave train | 1.669, against $k_{\mathrm{res}} = 1.5579$ (7 %) |

The control is steady to 1.4 parts in $10^4$ over 20000 steps and travels
exactly the distance the closed form says it should. The full run gives up 28 %
of its amplitude to radiation, and that radiation appears at the wavenumber the
dispersion relation predicts. The 7 % overshoot is consistent with the pulse
radiating while its own amplitude, and therefore its speed, is still changing.
@fig-kawahara-radiation shows the two runs' profiles directly, and is the
figure to read alongside this table: every number in the right-hand column is
visible in it.

## Governing equations

$$
\partial_t u \;+\; \alpha\,u\,\partial_x u
  \;-\; \beta\,\partial_x^3 u
  \;+\; \gamma\,\partial_x^5 u \;=\; 0 .
$$ {#eq-kw-pde}

::: {.callout-note}
## Sign convention

This application defines $\beta$ with a minus sign in @eq-kw-pde. To use a
coefficient $b$ multiplying $+u_{xxx}$, set $\beta = -b$.
:::

## Spectral formulation

Odd derivatives transform to odd powers of $ik$, so the symbol is **purely
imaginary**:

$$
L(k) \;=\; -i\,\omega(k), \qquad \omega(k) \;=\; \beta k^3 + \gamma k^5 .
$$ {#eq-kw-symbol}

The quadratic flux $\alpha u\,\partial_x u = \tfrac{\alpha}{2}\partial_x(u^2)$
is evaluated as $N = u^2$ with

$$
M_{\mathrm{nl}}(k) \;=\; -i\,\frac{\alpha}{2}\,k_x .
$$ {#eq-kw-nl}

This is the qualitative difference from every other spectral chapter here.
An even-order dissipative operator has $L$ real and negative: $|e^{L\Delta t}|<1$
and modes **decay**. Here $L$ is imaginary, so $|e^{L\Delta t}| = 1$ exactly and
modes **rotate** — the amplitude of each Fourier component is preserved and only
its phase advances. ETD is not damping anything; it is applying an exact phase
rotation.

The phase velocity follows from @eq-kw-symbol:

$$
c_p(k) \;=\; \frac{\omega(k)}{k} \;=\; \beta k^2 + \gamma k^4 ,
$$ {#eq-kw-phase}

which changes sign at $k^2 = -\beta/\gamma$ when $\beta\gamma < 0$. Below that
wave number waves travel one way, above it the other. The defaults
$\alpha = 1$, $\beta = 1$, $\gamma = -1$ put the model in this competing
regime.

## Solution strategy

ETD1 as in @eq-etd1, dealiased — the quadratic nonlinearity doubles the
highest wave number present, so the 2/3 rule is required.

## Verification

* **Phase velocity.** A single mode advances at $c_p(k)$ from
  @eq-kw-phase, checked independently for the $k^3$ and $k^5$ branches.
* **Manufactured solutions.** Independent manufactured-solution tests for
  third- and fifth-order dispersion.
* **Mean preservation.** The $\mathbf{k}=0$ mode is untouched — both terms in
  the PDE are $x$-derivatives, so this holds by construction; measured drift is
  a relative $2\times10^{-15}$.
* **Parameter mapping.** @eq-kw-map's coefficients and crossover are checked
  against hand-computed values.
* **Diagnostics self-test.** The envelope diagnostics recover the centroid,
  width and amplitude of a known static Gaussian-envelope carrier.
* **Group and phase velocity.** Measured against $d\omega/dk$ and $\omega/k$
  for carriers on both sides of the crossover, with the `edge_fraction`
  no-wrap check enforced automatically.
* **Solitary-wave control.** The $\gamma = 0$ run is asserted to be an exact
  KdV solitary wave — steady peak amplitude, closed-form speed, no wave train
  behind it — and switching $\gamma$ on is asserted to cost it 28 % of its
  amplitude, raise the trailing RMS 75-fold, and shed a wave train within 7 %
  of the resonant wavenumber.

## Binaries and inputs

`kawahara` (CPU), `kawahara_hip`. Verification preset `pulse.json`
(256-point line). Science presets
`wave_packet_below_crossover.json` / `wave_packet_above_crossover.json`
(case A) and `nonlinear_pulse_kdv_only.json` /
`nonlinear_pulse_kawahara.json` (case B). Both science cases are 1-D lines and
therefore single-rank: HeFFTe cannot split $N_y = N_z = 1$ across several
processes. The diagnostics and wave-packet path is CPU-only; it is not wired
onto the HIP session.

## Visualisation

![Two runs of the *same* solitary wave, differing only in $\gamma$, drawn as
line plots because this is the report's only one-dimensional application — a
$512\times1\times1$ snapshot rendered as an image would be a one-pixel stripe,
and the signal here is an amplitude. **Left**, the $\gamma = 0$ control. It is
an exact solution of the equation it is being integrated against, so the three
curves lie almost on top of each other: after 20000 steps the peak is unchanged
to 1.4 parts in $10^4$, the line either side of the pulse is flat, and the only
visible motion is the 2.50 length units the closed form says the wave should
travel. That is what makes the right-hand panel readable as physics rather than
as drift. **Right**, the same wave with $\gamma = 1/90$ restored. The pulse has
given up 28 % of its height by $t = 100$ and the line behind and ahead of it is
filled with a wave train at $k = 1.669$, within 7 % of the resonance
$c_p(k) = c$ at $k_{\mathrm{res}} = 1.5579$ that linear theory predicts and
that nothing in the solver is told. Note *where* the wave train sits: the
resonant waves have group velocity
$\mathrm{d}\omega/\mathrm{d}k = 3\beta k^2 + 5\gamma k^4 = 0.206$ at
$k_{\mathrm{res}}$, eight times the pulse's own speed $c = 0.025$, so the
radiation outruns its source and, by $t = 100$, has wrapped the periodic line —
which is why the observable is a whole-domain RMS and why no no-wrap claim is
made for this case. Both panels share one $u$ axis, so a millimetre is the same
amplitude in each.](figures/kawahara_solitary_radiation.svg){#fig-kawahara-radiation}

## Scalability

Not measured.
